choices.text: A normal required stage before rhythm conversion
choices.explanation: Neurological toxicity is not a desired treatment stage.

choices.text: Proof that the IV line is blocked
choices.explanation: The pattern does not establish mechanical line blockage.

lidocaine_product.stem: Which lidocaine product must be verified for an IV antiarrhythmic order?

choices.text: An IV antiarrhythmic preparation without unsuitable additives
choices.explanation: The exact route and product must be verified.

choices.text: A dental cartridge containing epinephrine
choices.explanation: Its additives and intended use may make it unsuitable.

choices.text: A topical solution with the same percentage
choices.explanation: A topical product is not interchangeable with an IV preparation.

choices.text: An injectable local mixture selected by total volume
choices.explanation: Total volume does not establish composition or IV suitability.

bicarbonate_selected.stem: Why should sodium bicarbonate not be given automatically in every cardiac arrest?

choices.text: It has selected indications rather than routine undifferentiated use
choices.explanation: Resuscitation follows the cause-specific guideline pathway.

choices.text: It replaces chest compressions when acidosis is suspected
choices.explanation: It does not replace high-quality CPR.

choices.text: A normal ECG always establishes its indication
choices.explanation: An ECG alone does not establish a bicarbonate indication.

choices.text: It removes the need to investigate reversible causes
choices.explanation: Cause assessment remains essential.

bicarbonate_load.stem: After excessive bicarbonate exposure, what should be considered?

choices.text: Alkalemia and sodium/volume burden
choices.explanation: These can result from excessive administration.

choices.text: Guaranteed removal of all excess body potassium
choices.explanation: Bicarbonate does not guarantee potassium removal.

choices.text: A permanent inability to develop acidosis
choices.explanation: Acid-base disorders can recur or persist.

choices.text: A lack of any need for reassessment
choices.explanation: Acid-base, electrolyte and volume status need monitoring.

hydralazine_reflex.stem: BP falls after hydralazine while the pulse accelerates. Which mechanism can explain this?

choices.text: Reflex tachycardia after arteriolar dilation
choices.explanation: A pressure fall can trigger a compensatory heart-rate rise.

choices.text: Direct beta-receptor blockade
choices.explanation: Hydralazine is not a beta blocker.

choices.text: Complete suppression of sympathetic reflexes
choices.explanation: Reflex activation can still occur.

choices.text: Replacement of circulating glucose
choices.explanation: This is not its principal pharmacological action.

dextrose_site.stem: A dextrose infusion site becomes swollen and painful. What should happen first?

choices.text: Stop delivery through the affected site and assess extravasation
choices.explanation: Concentrated dextrose can injure tissue outside the vein.

choices.text: Flush the site forcefully and continue
choices.explanation: This may worsen local exposure.

choices.text: Cover swelling and wait until the dose is complete
choices.explanation: Continued delivery can worsen injury.

choices.text: Massage before assessing line patency
choices.explanation: This does not safely address extravasation.

dextrose_units.stem: A label states dextrose 50% w/v. How much dextrose is contained in 20 mL?

choices.explanation: 50 g per 100 mL gives 10 g in 20 mL.

choices.text: 1 g
choices.explanation: This treats the concentration as 5% rather than 50%.
This assumes 1 g per mL instead of 0.5 g per mL.
That amount is in 100 mL, not 20 mL.

unconscious_airway.stem: An unconscious hypoglycemic patient cannot swallow safely. What must be avoided?

choices.text: Giving oral glucose or fluid into the mouth
choices.explanation: Reduced consciousness creates aspiration risk.

choices.text: Calling for urgent assistance
choices.explanation: Urgent assistance is appropriate.

choices.text: Assessing airway and breathing
choices.explanation: Airway and breathing assessment is essential.

choices.text: Using the authorized non-oral rescue pathway
choices.explanation: Non-oral treatment is appropriate when swallowing is unsafe.

steroid_glucose.stem: During systemic corticosteroid treatment, glucose rises above the patient's usual pattern. What should be considered?

choices.text: A steroid-related increase needing monitoring and plan review
choices.explanation: Glucocorticoids can increase glucose.

choices.text: Proof that corticosteroids lower glucose
choices.explanation: The usual metabolic risk is hyperglycemia.

choices.text: A reason to stop all glucose checks
choices.explanation: The change supports monitoring rather than stopping it.

choices.text: A finding explained only by insulin overdose
choices.explanation: Excess insulin usually lowers glucose.

steroid_infection.stem: Why should infection surveillance continue during systemic steroid treatment?

choices.text: Steroids can increase infection risk and affect healing
choices.explanation: Clinical vigilance remains important.

choices.text: Steroids sterilize an infected wound
choices.explanation: They are not antimicrobial treatment.

choices.text: Reduced inflammation always means the pathogen is gone
choices.explanation: Suppressed inflammatory signs do not prove eradication.

choices.text: The infection risk ends after the first dose
choices.explanation: Risk depends on regimen and patient context.

steroid_adrenal.stem: A patient on prolonged prednisolone wants to stop abruptly. What is the concern?

choices.text: Adrenal suppression may require an authorized withdrawal plan
choices.explanation: Abrupt cessation after prolonged exposure can be unsafe.

choices.text: Every course can be stopped identically
choices.explanation: Duration, dose and clinical context matter.

choices.text: The medicine permanently replaces all stress responses
choices.explanation: Adrenal function can be suppressed rather than permanently supported.

choices.text: Stopping abruptly prevents all steroid complications
choices.explanation: Unplanned withdrawal can introduce serious risk.

steroid_anaphylaxis.stem: In suspected anaphylaxis, which statement about hydrocortisone is correct?

choices.text: It must not delay epinephrine and immediate emergency care
choices.explanation: It is not the first lifesaving treatment for airway or circulatory compromise.

choices.text: It replaces epinephrine when the patient is hypotensive
choices.explanation: It does not provide equivalent immediate rescue.

choices.text: It works quickly enough to postpone airway support
choices.explanation: Airway compromise needs immediate management.

choices.text: It removes the need for monitoring after symptoms improve
choices.explanation: Ongoing reassessment remains important.

calcium_no_k_removal.stem: After IV calcium for hyperkalemic ECG toxicity, the tracing improves. What remains necessary?

choices.text: Treatment and monitoring of the elevated potassium
choices.explanation: Calcium stabilizes the myocardium but does not remove potassium.

choices.text: Assume the total body potassium has been removed
choices.explanation: ECG stabilization is not potassium removal.

choices.text: Stop checking potassium because the QRS improved
choices.explanation: The potassium hazard can persist.

choices.text: Use the ECG change to calculate the new potassium exactly
choices.explanation: ECG appearance cannot precisely quantify serum potassium.

calcium_bicarbonate.stem: Why should calcium and bicarbonate not be mixed without verified compatibility?

choices.text: They may form a precipitate when mixed
choices.explanation: This is a clinically important physical incompatibility.

choices.text: They only need to have the same labelled strength
choices.explanation: Matching strengths does not establish compatibility.

choices.text: A slow injection makes every mixture compatible
choices.explanation: Slower delivery does not prevent chemical incompatibility.

choices.text: Clear separate solutions are sufficient proof of compatibility
choices.explanation: Precipitation can occur after the solutions meet.

calcium_salts.stem: Why is equal volume substitution between calcium gluconate and calcium chloride unsafe?

choices.text: Their elemental calcium contents differ
choices.explanation: Dose equivalence requires checking the specific salts and concentrations.

choices.text: Both salts always provide identical calcium per mL
choices.explanation: They do not have universal volume equivalence.

choices.text: Salt names affect packaging only
choices.explanation: The salt affects the supplied elemental calcium.

choices.text: Only the syringe size determines elemental calcium
choices.explanation: Product concentration and salt are essential.

magnesium_indication.stem: Which arrhythmia most specifically matches magnesium's taught role?

choices.text: Torsades de pointes associated with long QT
choices.explanation: Magnesium has an indication-specific role here.

choices.text: Every cardiac arrest regardless of rhythm
choices.explanation: Routine use in undifferentiated arrest is not recommended.

choices.text: Every normal sinus rhythm
choices.explanation: Normal sinus rhythm is not itself an indication.

choices.text: All asymptomatic bradycardias
choices.explanation: Bradycardia alone does not establish a magnesium indication.

magnesium_toxicity.stem: During magnesium infusion, reflexes disappear and breathing slows. What is the priority?

choices.text: Stop administration and obtain emergency toxicity assessment
choices.explanation: Respiratory depression and reflex loss are important toxicity signs.

choices.text: Increase infusion because absent reflexes prove benefit
choices.explanation: These findings can signal dangerous toxicity.

choices.text: Wait for the next scheduled magnesium result alone
choices.explanation: Clinical respiratory deterioration needs immediate action.

choices.text: Ask the patient to walk to restore reflexes
choices.explanation: Mobilization is unsafe and does not treat toxicity.

magnesium_calcium.stem: Which treatment should be anticipated under the emergency plan for important magnesium toxicity?

choices.text: An authorized IV calcium salt
choices.explanation: Calcium can antagonize magnesium's toxic effects.

choices.text: An additional magnesium bolus
choices.explanation: More magnesium can worsen toxicity.

choices.text: An oral multivitamin as immediate rescue
choices.explanation: It does not provide appropriate acute antagonism.

choices.text: A routine extra loop-diuretic dose without assessment
choices.explanation: Treatment requires an authorized toxicity plan and supportive care.

digoxin_toxicity.stem: A patient on digoxin develops nausea, visual symptoms and a new slow irregular pulse. What is most appropriate?

choices.text: Assess for digoxin toxicity and escalate
choices.explanation: Gastrointestinal, neurological and rhythm findings can occur together.

choices.text: Treat nausea alone and give the next dose automatically
choices.explanation: The combined pattern requires medication and rhythm review.

choices.text: Exclude toxicity because the medicine was previously tolerated
choices.explanation: Renal change and interactions can alter exposure.

choices.text: Use the normal temperature to dismiss the symptoms
choices.explanation: Temperature does not establish digoxin safety.

digoxin_interaction.stem: Why is a new amiodarone order important in a patient already receiving digoxin?

choices.text: It can increase digoxin exposure and compound cardiac slowing
choices.explanation: The combination needs dose/monitoring review.

choices.text: It guarantees lower digoxin concentrations
choices.explanation: Exposure may rise rather than fall.

choices.text: It removes the need to check the pulse
choices.explanation: Cardiac slowing makes pulse and rhythm assessment important.

choices.text: It makes renal function irrelevant
choices.explanation: Renal function remains relevant to digoxin safety.

aminophylline_toxicity.stem: A patient on aminophylline develops vomiting, tremor and tachyarrhythmia. What should be considered?

choices.text: Concentration-related toxicity
choices.explanation: Aminophylline has a narrow therapeutic index.

choices.text: A desired response proving ideal bronchodilation
choices.explanation: These findings can represent toxicity, not treatment success.

choices.text: A reason to omit rhythm assessment
choices.explanation: Arrhythmia needs prompt clinical assessment.

choices.text: An effect excluded by a previously normal concentration
choices.explanation: Exposure can change and an old level may no longer apply.

aminophylline_exposure.stem: Before aminophylline is prescribed, what prior treatment information is especially relevant?

choices.text: Recent theophylline or aminophylline doses
choices.explanation: Prior methylxanthine exposure affects accumulation risk.

choices.text: Only the last inhaled bronchodilator time
choices.explanation: This does not establish the existing methylxanthine burden.

choices.text: Only whether the patient currently has wheeze
choices.explanation: Symptoms do not quantify prior drug exposure.

choices.text: Only the admission respiratory rate
choices.explanation: A baseline observation does not establish recent systemic dosing.

tca_cardiac.stem: Why does recent MI matter when reviewing amitriptyline?

choices.text: TCAs can affect cardiac conduction and are unsuitable in acute MI recovery
choices.explanation: This is a clinically important cardiac safety issue.

choices.text: TCAs prevent every post-MI dysrhythmia
choices.explanation: They can instead worsen conduction and toxicity risks.

choices.text: Amitriptyline has no cardiac effects
choices.explanation: Its cardiac effects are important.

choices.text: Recent MI determines only the tablet's coating
choices.explanation: The concern is physiological safety, not coating.

tca_overdose.stem: Suspected amitriptyline overdose is accompanied by QRS widening and hypotension. What is the priority?

choices.text: Urgent monitored toxicology/emergency assessment
choices.explanation: TCA overdose can cause life-threatening conduction and circulatory toxicity.

choices.text: Routine reassurance because it is an antidepressant
choices.explanation: Its usual indication does not make overdose benign.

choices.text: Waiting for mood symptoms before escalation
choices.explanation: Cardiac toxicity can be an immediate threat.

choices.text: Giving the next regular dose while awaiting review
choices.explanation: Further exposure is inappropriate in suspected overdose.

multivitamin_contents.stem: Two products are both labelled multivitamin. What determines whether they duplicate treatment?

choices.text: Compare the actual ingredients and strengths
choices.explanation: Products labelled multivitamin may have different compositions.

choices.text: Match the number of tablets recommended daily
choices.explanation: Tablet count does not identify the ingredient amounts.

choices.text: Assume equivalent content from the shared product category
choices.explanation: Multivitamin is not a standardized composition.

choices.text: Compare only the amounts of one shared vitamin
choices.explanation: Other vitamins and minerals may still differ or overlap.

multivitamin_duplicate.stem: A patient takes two multivitamins plus a separate vitamin supplement. What should be reviewed?

choices.text: Add overlapping ingredient amounts across all products
choices.explanation: Several supplements can duplicate exposure.

choices.text: Review only the prescribed multivitamin
choices.explanation: Other supplements also contribute doses.

choices.text: Count each product against its own label independently
choices.explanation: This can miss a combined excessive intake.

choices.text: Assume separate administration times avoid duplication
choices.explanation: Time separation does not remove the total nutrient exposure.

multivitamin_absorption.stem: A mineral-containing supplement is taken with a medicine affected by chelation. What should be checked?

choices.text: Check mineral ingredients and product-specific separation advice
choices.explanation: Chelation can reduce absorption of susceptible medicines.

choices.text: Keep the doses together if both are taken with food
choices.explanation: Food does not necessarily prevent the interaction.

choices.text: Use a double antibiotic dose to compensate without an order
choices.explanation: Improvised dose changes are unsafe.

choices.text: Apply one separation interval to every drug and supplement
choices.explanation: Recommendations are medicine- and product-specific.

alteplase_screen.stem: Before stroke thrombolysis, why must brain imaging be reviewed?

choices.text: To exclude intracranial hemorrhage and assess eligibility
choices.explanation: A hemorrhagic stroke must not be treated as an eligible ischemic stroke.

choices.text: To guarantee every suspected stroke receives alteplase
choices.explanation: Imaging is part of selection, not automatic treatment.

choices.text: To replace the clinical and timing assessment
choices.explanation: Eligibility also depends on the full clinical context.

choices.text: To calculate the dose without a patient weight
choices.explanation: Imaging does not provide the required weight-based dose.

alteplase_neuro.stem: During alteplase infusion, the patient develops sudden severe headache and neurological worsening. What is the priority?

choices.text: Stop the infusion and activate urgent neurological/bleeding assessment
choices.explanation: Acute deterioration can indicate intracranial bleeding.

choices.text: Complete the infusion before reporting
choices.explanation: Continuing while delaying assessment can worsen harm.

choices.text: Give an antiplatelet immediately without a new order
choices.explanation: Urgent assessment and the post-thrombolysis protocol are required.

choices.text: Treat it as expected proof of clot dissolution
choices.explanation: Neurological worsening is a red flag, not a desired response.

alteplase_regimen.stem: Why must the indication be checked before preparing alteplase?

choices.text: The indication determines the appropriate dose and schedule
choices.explanation: Stroke, MI and PE regimens differ.

choices.text: The same vial permits copying any previous regimen
choices.explanation: A shared vial does not make regimens interchangeable.

choices.text: The available bag size alone determines the dose
choices.explanation: The prescribed indication and patient factors guide dosing.

choices.text: The last patient's infusion duration is sufficient
choices.explanation: Another patient's indication may require a different regimen.

alteplase_timing.stem: A possible stroke patient's onset time is unclear. What should be communicated promptly?

choices.text: Last-known-well and the circumstances of discovery
choices.explanation: Eligibility uses current stroke guidance and the applicable pathway.

choices.text: Only the time the hospital chart was opened
choices.explanation: That may differ greatly from last-known-well.

choices.text: Only the time the family called a taxi
choices.explanation: This does not establish neurological onset.

choices.text: An estimated time invented to fit a treatment window
choices.explanation: Uncertain history must not be replaced with invented timing.

ccu-lesson-01-acs.point: Distinguish unstable angina from infarction by myocardial injury.
ccu-lesson-01-acs.stem: A patient has acute ischemic symptoms but no biomarker evidence of myocardial necrosis after appropriate assessment. Which ACS category fits that distinction?

choices.text: Unstable angina
choices.explanation: It involves ischemia without biomarker evidence of necrosis.

choices.text: NSTEMI
choices.explanation: NSTEMI requires myocardial infarction, not ischemia alone.

choices.text: STEMI
choices.explanation: This is an infarction category with a compatible ST-elevation presentation.

choices.text: Complete heart block
choices.explanation: This is a conduction disorder, not an ACS category.

ccu-lesson-01-acs.point: NSTEMI can occur without persistent ST elevation.
ccu-lesson-01-acs.stem: Ischemic symptoms accompany myocardial injury, but there is no persistent ST elevation. Which interpretation is appropriate?

choices.text: NSTEMI remains possible
choices.explanation: Infarction does not require persistent ST elevation.

choices.text: Myocardial infarction is excluded
choices.explanation: That would incorrectly exclude NSTEMI.

choices.text: Only stable angina is possible
choices.explanation: Established myocardial injury is not explained by stable angina alone.

choices.text: The result establishes asystole
choices.explanation: Asystole is an arrest rhythm, not this diagnostic distinction.

ccu-lesson-01-acs.point: Escalate concerning ischemia without waiting for biomarkers.
ccu-lesson-01-acs.stem: A patient develops chest pressure, sweating and a falling BP while troponin is pending. What takes priority?

choices.text: Immediate assessment, monitoring and escalation
choices.explanation: Hemodynamic deterioration must not wait for biomarkers.

choices.text: Waiting for the laboratory result before contacting the team
choices.explanation: Delay is unsafe in an unstable ischemic presentation.

choices.text: Completing routine discharge teaching first
choices.explanation: Urgent clinical assessment takes priority.

choices.text: Reassuring the patient because infarction is not yet proven
choices.explanation: Uncertainty does not remove the need for urgent assessment.

ccu-lesson-01-acs.point: A 12-lead ECG supports prompt ACS assessment.
ccu-lesson-01-acs.stem: Which investigation should be obtained promptly alongside bedside assessment when ACS is suspected?

choices.text: A diagnostic 12-lead ECG
choices.explanation: This promptly assesses ischemic and rhythm changes.

choices.text: A routine rhythm strip as the only ECG assessment
choices.explanation: A monitoring strip does not replace diagnostic views.

choices.text: An exercise test before urgent evaluation
choices.explanation: Acute concerning symptoms require immediate assessment.

choices.text: A repeat troponin before any ECG
choices.explanation: Do not delay the ECG while waiting for biomarkers.

ccu-lesson-02-chb.point: Recognize AV dissociation rather than conducted sinus bradycardia.
ccu-lesson-02-chb.stem: A slow tracing shows regular P waves and regular QRS complexes at independent rates. Which explanation fits?

choices.text: Atrial impulses are not conducting to the ventricles
choices.explanation: Independent atrial and ventricular activity supports complete block.

choices.text: Every P wave conducts with a fixed PR interval
choices.explanation: That contradicts the described independence.

choices.text: The ventricles are electrically silent
choices.explanation: QRS complexes are present.

choices.text: The pulse rate must equal the atrial rate
choices.explanation: An independent ventricular escape rhythm can be much slower.

ccu-lesson-02-chb.point: Poor perfusion in CHB requires rapid escalation and pacing readiness.
ccu-lesson-02-chb.stem: A patient with complete heart block becomes confused and hypotensive. What should the nurse prioritize?

choices.text: Support ABCs, escalate and prepare for pacing
choices.explanation: Poor perfusion makes this an urgent symptomatic block.

choices.text: Wait for the rhythm to become fast before calling
choices.explanation: Severe bradycardia can already compromise output.

choices.text: Use the P-wave rate to judge perfusion as adequate
choices.explanation: The ventricular response and patient condition matter.

choices.text: Leave the patient for routine oral medication collection
choices.explanation: An unstable patient needs ongoing monitoring and support.

ccu-lesson-02-chb.point: Review rate-slowing drugs in CHB assessment.
ccu-lesson-02-chb.stem: Which medication history is especially relevant when investigating new complete heart block?

choices.text: Beta blocker, verapamil or digoxin exposure
choices.explanation: These medicines can impair conduction.

choices.text: A local oral antifungal alone
choices.explanation: It is not the highlighted AV-node-slowing group.

choices.text: An occasional multivitamin alone
choices.explanation: It does not establish nodal depression.

choices.text: A stool-softening regimen alone
choices.explanation: It does not explain AV-conduction suppression.

ccu-lesson-03-12lead-ecg.point: Distinguish physical electrodes from derived ECG leads.
ccu-lesson-03-12lead-ecg.stem: A complete diagnostic ECG is recorded using ten stickers. Why can it display twelve leads?

choices.text: Leads are electrical views derived from the electrodes
choices.explanation: The number of views differs from physical contacts.

choices.text: Each sticker must represent exactly one displayed lead
choices.explanation: That would incorrectly equate electrode and lead.

choices.text: Two stickers are missing from the recording
choices.explanation: Ten electrodes are the normal physical setup.

choices.text: Two of the displayed views are pulse-oximeter waveforms
choices.explanation: ECG leads do not come from the pulse-oximeter probe.

ccu-lesson-03-12lead-ecg.point: Place V1 and V2 at the fourth intercostal space.
ccu-lesson-03-12lead-ecg.stem: V1 and V2 have been placed in the second intercostal space. What should be corrected?

choices.text: Move them to the fourth intercostal space at the respective sternal borders
choices.explanation: High placement can create misleading changes.

choices.text: Keep them because only limb electrodes affect the tracing
choices.explanation: Chest electrode position affects the recorded views.

choices.text: Move both to the fifth space at the midaxillary line
choices.explanation: That is not the correct V1/V2 position.

choices.text: Move them to the same point as V4
choices.explanation: Each chest position has a defined anatomical location.

ccu-lesson-03-12lead-ecg.point: V5 and V6 stay horizontally level with V4.
ccu-lesson-03-12lead-ecg.stem: After finding V4, how should V5 and V6 be positioned?

choices.text: At V4's horizontal level along their specified axillary lines
choices.explanation: Do not follow a descending rib to place them lower.

choices.text: One intercostal space lower for each successive electrode
choices.explanation: They remain horizontally level with V4.

choices.text: Both at the left sternal border
choices.explanation: Their landmarks are axillary rather than sternal.

choices.text: Both halfway between V2 and V4
choices.explanation: That describes V3's relationship, not V5/V6.

ccu-lesson-03-12lead-ecg.point: The T wave represents ventricular repolarization.
ccu-lesson-03-12lead-ecg.stem: Which waveform represents the ventricles recovering electrically after depolarization?

choices.text: T wave
choices.explanation: It represents ventricular repolarization.

choices.text: P wave
choices.explanation: It represents atrial depolarization.

choices.text: QRS complex
choices.explanation: It represents ventricular depolarization.

choices.text: Pacing spike
choices.explanation: It represents an artificial electrical stimulus.

ccu-lesson-03-12lead-ecg.point: Use the stated IEC limb-electrode convention.
ccu-lesson-03-12lead-ecg.stem: Using the IEC colour convention, which electrode is the neutral right-leg connection?

choices.text: Black, RL/N
choices.explanation: N denotes neutral in this convention.

choices.text: Green, LL/F
choices.explanation: This is the left-leg or foot connection.

choices.text: Yellow, LA/L
choices.explanation: This is the left-arm connection.

choices.text: Red, RA/R
choices.explanation: This is the right-arm connection.

ccu-lesson-04-telemetry.point: Telemetry is rhythm monitoring rather than diagnostic 12-lead ECG.
ccu-lesson-04-telemetry.stem: A patient with new ischemic chest pain already has bedside telemetry. Which statement is correct?

choices.text: Telemetry does not replace an indicated diagnostic 12-lead ECG
choices.explanation: Continuous rhythm surveillance and diagnostic views have different roles.

choices.text: Telemetry always provides the same twelve diagnostic views
choices.explanation: A routine monitoring setup does not do this.

choices.text: A pulse-oximeter pleth replaces all ECG assessment
choices.explanation: Pleth measures pulsatile flow rather than cardiac electrical views.

choices.text: A displayed rate excludes myocardial ischemia
choices.explanation: Rate alone cannot exclude ischemia.

ccu-lesson-04-telemetry.point: Pleth reflects pulsatile blood flow rather than electrical activity.
ccu-lesson-04-telemetry.stem: The pulse-oximeter pleth disappears while the ECG still displays complexes. What must be assessed?

choices.text: The patient, pulse and probe/perfusion status
choices.explanation: Electrical activity does not guarantee a usable peripheral pulse signal.

choices.text: Only the ECG print speed
choices.explanation: Print speed does not establish circulation or probe contact.

choices.text: Whether every QRS guarantees a palpable pulse
choices.explanation: Electrical complexes can exist without effective circulation.

choices.text: Whether the ECG electrodes also generate the pleth
choices.explanation: The pleth comes from the pulse-oximeter probe.

ccu-lesson-04-telemetry.point: Estimate rate from QRS count on a six-second strip.
ccu-lesson-04-telemetry.stem: There are nine QRS complexes on a six-second rhythm strip. What is the approximate ventricular rate?

choices.text: 90/min
choices.explanation: Nine multiplied by ten gives about 90/min.

choices.text: 54/min
choices.explanation: This incorrectly multiplies by six.

choices.text: 60/min
choices.explanation: This ignores the counted complexes.

choices.text: 150/min
choices.explanation: This does not follow the six-second calculation.

ccu-lesson-04-telemetry.point: Check the patient and pulse before treating suspected artifact.
ccu-lesson-04-telemetry.stem: The monitor appears chaotic while the patient talks normally with a strong regular pulse. What comes first?

choices.text: Assess the patient and check electrodes for artifact
choices.explanation: Clinical findings and equipment assessment help avoid treating artifact.

choices.text: Deliver a shock solely from the screen image
choices.explanation: A monitor appearance alone is not enough in this situation.

choices.text: Declare cardiac arrest despite the strong pulse
choices.explanation: Arrest requires loss of effective circulation.

choices.text: Disconnect all monitoring and leave
choices.explanation: The tracing still needs safe assessment and correction.

ccu-lesson-05-dangerous-rhythms.point: Pulse status changes the VT treatment pathway.
ccu-lesson-05-dangerous-rhythms.stem: Why must pulse status be checked promptly when VT is seen?

choices.text: Pulseless VT and VT with a pulse use different pathways
choices.explanation: Circulation determines arrest versus peri-arrest management.

choices.text: Every VT rhythm receives the same treatment
choices.explanation: Pulse and instability change treatment selection.

choices.text: VT always has a palpable pulse
choices.explanation: VT can be pulseless.

choices.text: VT never causes circulatory compromise
choices.explanation: VT can cause shock or arrest.

ccu-lesson-05-dangerous-rhythms.point: PEA is non-shockable organized electrical activity without a pulse.
ccu-lesson-05-dangerous-rhythms.stem: An unresponsive patient has organized ECG complexes but no definite pulse. Which interpretation fits?

choices.text: Pulseless electrical activity
choices.explanation: PEA is defined by absent effective circulation despite electrical activity.

choices.text: A stable perfusing rhythm
choices.explanation: Electrical appearance does not prove perfusion.

choices.text: Ventricular fibrillation
choices.explanation: VF does not show organized complexes as described.

choices.text: Sinus bradycardia with adequate circulation
choices.explanation: The absence of a pulse excludes adequate circulation.

ccu-lesson-05-dangerous-rhythms.stem: Which pair should be selected as shockable cardiac-arrest rhythms?

choices.text: VF and pulseless VT
choices.explanation: Both use the shockable arrest pathway.

choices.text: PEA and asystole
choices.explanation: These are non-shockable arrest rhythms.

choices.text: Asystole and VF
choices.explanation: Only VF in this pair is shockable.

choices.text: PEA and pulseless VT
choices.explanation: Only pulseless VT in this pair is shockable.

ccu-lesson-06-electrical-treatment.point: Synchronize a shock to avoid the vulnerable T-wave period.
ccu-lesson-06-electrical-treatment.stem: Why is synchronization used for indicated cardioversion of a tachyarrhythmia with a pulse?

choices.text: To time the shock with the R wave
choices.explanation: This avoids delivering it during the vulnerable T-wave period.

choices.text: To deliver the shock specifically on the T wave
choices.explanation: That would increase proarrhythmic risk.

choices.text: To guarantee painless treatment without sedation
choices.explanation: Synchronization does not provide analgesia or sedation.

choices.text: To convert every shock into pacing
choices.explanation: Cardioversion and pacing are different interventions.

ccu-lesson-06-electrical-treatment.point: Polymorphic VT requiring shock uses an unsynchronized shock.
ccu-lesson-06-electrical-treatment.stem: Polymorphic VT requires an immediate shock. Why is reliable synchronization problematic?

choices.text: The changing QRS pattern prevents dependable synchronization
choices.explanation: Use the indicated unsynchronized shock pathway.

choices.text: The presence of a pulse makes any shock impossible
choices.explanation: Some tachyarrhythmias with a pulse require urgent shocks.

choices.text: A pacing spike must be inserted before each shock
choices.explanation: That is not the defining requirement.

choices.text: Polymorphic VT is always a non-shockable rhythm
choices.explanation: It can require defibrillation.

ccu-lesson-06-electrical-treatment.point: Confirm mechanical capture as well as electrical capture.
ccu-lesson-06-electrical-treatment.stem: Pacing spikes are followed by QRS complexes, but the patient remains hypotensive. What must be checked?

choices.text: A corresponding pulse and perfusion response
choices.explanation: Electrical capture alone does not establish effective mechanical capture.

choices.text: Whether the spikes are visually symmetrical
choices.explanation: Spike appearance does not prove output.

choices.text: Whether the monitor displays the programmed pacing rate
choices.explanation: A displayed rate does not guarantee perfusion.

choices.text: Whether all further clinical checks can stop
choices.explanation: Persistent hypotension requires reassessment.

ccu-lesson-06-electrical-treatment.point: Choose electrical treatment using pulse and rate-related instability.
ccu-lesson-06-electrical-treatment.stem: Which electrical support best matches dangerous symptomatic bradycardia from high-grade block?

choices.text: Pacing
choices.explanation: Repeated stimulation can support a dangerously slow ventricular response.

choices.text: Synchronized cardioversion of the slow rhythm
choices.explanation: Cardioversion is used for selected tachyarrhythmias.

choices.text: Routine defibrillation of a perfusing slow rhythm
choices.explanation: Defibrillation is not routine treatment for this bradycardia.

choices.text: No intervention because a pulse is present
choices.explanation: A pulse does not make severe symptomatic bradycardia safe.

ccu-lesson-07-sudden-deterioration.point: Assess the patient with ABCDE during sudden deterioration.
ccu-lesson-07-sudden-deterioration.stem: A previously alert patient becomes confused and breathless. What should the nurse do first?

choices.text: Go to the bedside and perform an immediate ABCDE assessment
choices.explanation: Start with the patient's current airway, breathing and circulation.

choices.text: Read the old discharge summary before assessing
choices.explanation: Historical detail must not delay current assessment.

choices.text: Wait for a monitor alarm to confirm deterioration
choices.explanation: Clinical deterioration may precede or occur without an alarm.

choices.text: Finish routine documentation before checking the patient
choices.explanation: Urgent assessment takes priority.

ccu-lesson-07-sudden-deterioration.point: New shock signs require prompt escalation.
ccu-lesson-07-sudden-deterioration.stem: Which combination requires urgent escalation rather than routine observation?

choices.text: New confusion, cold clammy skin and falling BP
choices.explanation: These are signs of possible poor perfusion.

choices.text: Stable BP, normal alertness and unchanged breathing
choices.explanation: This does not describe new deterioration.

choices.text: Unchanged chronic edema without new symptoms
choices.explanation: This is less urgent than new shock signs.

choices.text: A request to adjust the pillow with stable observations
choices.explanation: Comfort needs differ from acute instability.

ccu-lesson-07-sudden-deterioration.point: Reassess after intervention rather than assuming benefit.
ccu-lesson-07-sudden-deterioration.stem: After an urgent intervention, which action completes the immediate nursing cycle?

choices.text: Repeat relevant observations and assess the response
choices.explanation: Treatment must be checked for benefit and adverse effects.

choices.text: Assume completion proves the problem resolved
choices.explanation: An intervention can fail or create complications.

choices.text: Stop documenting changes once help arrives
choices.explanation: Changes, actions and response remain important.

choices.text: Wait until the next shift to check effectiveness
choices.explanation: Deterioration needs timely reassessment.

ccu-lesson-08-cardiogenic-shock.point: Weak pump function can cause organ hypoperfusion.
ccu-lesson-08-cardiogenic-shock.stem: After MI, a patient has hypotension, cold extremities, confusion and oliguria. What unifies these findings?

choices.text: Inadequate cardiac output causing organ hypoperfusion
choices.explanation: This is the core cardiogenic-shock concern.

choices.text: Adequate circulation because the heart is still beating
choices.explanation: A heartbeat does not guarantee sufficient output.

choices.text: Isolated peripheral edema without perfusion effects
choices.explanation: Several organ-perfusion signs are abnormal.

choices.text: Improved renal perfusion from the pressure fall
choices.explanation: Hypotension with oliguria suggests the opposite.

ccu-lesson-08-cardiogenic-shock.point: Large automatic fluid boluses can worsen pump-failure congestion.
ccu-lesson-08-cardiogenic-shock.stem: A hypotensive patient has weak pump function and pulmonary crackles. Why must a large fluid bolus not be assumed appropriate?

choices.text: Additional fluid can worsen pulmonary congestion
choices.explanation: The full hemodynamic picture needs an authorized treatment plan.

choices.text: Every hypotensive patient is necessarily volume depleted
choices.explanation: Hypotension has several causes, including pump failure.

choices.text: Crackles prove that the circulation contains no fluid
choices.explanation: Crackles can reflect pulmonary congestion.

choices.text: Fluid always strengthens myocardial contraction directly
choices.explanation: Volume loading does not repair intrinsic contractile failure.

ccu-lesson-08-cardiogenic-shock.point: Use history and the whole examination to distinguish shock patterns.
ccu-lesson-08-cardiogenic-shock.stem: Which picture more strongly supports hypovolemia than pump failure?

choices.text: Recent major fluid loss, flat neck veins and clear lungs
choices.explanation: Together these support an empty-tank pattern.

choices.text: Pulmonary crackles with raised JVP and weak output
choices.explanation: This more strongly suggests congestion with pump failure.

choices.text: A low BP result without any other findings
choices.explanation: BP alone cannot distinguish the mechanism.

choices.text: Tachycardia alone
choices.explanation: It can occur in several shock states.

ccu-lesson-08-cardiogenic-shock.point: Track organ perfusion alongside BP in shock.
ccu-lesson-08-cardiogenic-shock.stem: Which trend is particularly important alongside BP during shock reassessment?

choices.text: Consciousness and urine output
choices.explanation: These reflect cerebral and renal perfusion.

choices.text: The prescribed pump rate without patient reassessment
choices.explanation: A correct setting does not establish organ response.

choices.text: Heart rate without other observations
choices.explanation: Rate alone does not establish sufficient output.

choices.text: A single SpO2 reading without circulatory findings
choices.explanation: Oxygen saturation does not establish organ blood flow.

ccu-lesson-09-norepi-dobutamine.point: Distinguish vascular pressure support from contractility support.
ccu-lesson-09-norepi-dobutamine.stem: Why might norepinephrine and dobutamine be used together?

choices.text: One supports vascular pressure while the other supports contractility
choices.explanation: They address different components of circulatory failure.

choices.text: Both are simply two brands of the same drug
choices.explanation: They have different principal actions.

choices.text: Both reduce cardiac contraction to the same extent
choices.explanation: Dobutamine principally increases contractile support.

choices.text: One replaces all monitoring required by the other
choices.explanation: Both require close hemodynamic monitoring.

ccu-lesson-09-norepi-dobutamine.point: Assess perfusion and rhythm during vasoactive treatment.
ccu-lesson-09-norepi-dobutamine.stem: During dobutamine support, HR rises markedly without better perfusion. What is appropriate?

choices.text: Reassess rhythm, BP and organ response and report
choices.explanation: More tachycardia does not guarantee improved output.

choices.text: Assume faster HR proves effective pump support
choices.explanation: Excessive rate can be harmful.

choices.text: Judge effectiveness from pump settings alone
choices.explanation: Device settings do not establish clinical response.

choices.text: Stop measuring urine because BP is displayed
choices.explanation: Organ response remains relevant.

ccu-lesson-09-norepi-dobutamine.point: Infusion rates depend on dose and concentration.
ccu-lesson-09-norepi-dobutamine.stem: Why is memorizing one universal mL/hour rate unsafe for vasoactive infusions?

choices.text: The rate changes with prescribed dose and prepared concentration
choices.explanation: mL/hour alone does not specify drug delivery.

choices.text: Every prepared bag has identical concentration
choices.explanation: Preparation can vary.

choices.text: The same rate always produces the same patient response
choices.explanation: Dose and physiological response vary.

choices.text: A pump setting removes the need to read the order
choices.explanation: The pump must be set against a verified prescription.

ccu-lesson-10-electrolytes.point: Hyperkalemia with ECG change needs urgent monitoring and escalation.
ccu-lesson-10-electrolytes.stem: Potassium is high and QRS complexes are widening. What takes priority?

choices.text: Continuous monitoring and urgent clinical escalation
choices.explanation: ECG toxicity can precede life-threatening arrhythmia.

choices.text: Waiting for loss of pulse before reporting
choices.explanation: Escalation should occur before arrest.

choices.text: Treating the result as harmless if the patient can speak
choices.explanation: Alertness does not exclude electrical toxicity.

choices.text: A routine repeat next week
choices.explanation: The ECG change makes this an urgent problem.

ccu-lesson-10-electrolytes.point: Low magnesium can make hypokalemia harder to correct.
ccu-lesson-10-electrolytes.stem: Potassium remains low despite replacement in a patient with ventricular ectopy. Which associated result should be reviewed?

choices.text: Magnesium
choices.explanation: Magnesium depletion can contribute to persistent hypokalemia.

choices.text: An isolated normal bilirubin
choices.explanation: It does not assess the highlighted electrolyte relationship.

choices.text: The platelet count alone
choices.explanation: Platelets do not establish magnesium status.

choices.text: An old serum cholesterol result
choices.explanation: It does not guide this acute electrolyte problem.

ccu-lesson-10-electrolytes.point: Calcium abnormalities can change the QT interval.
ccu-lesson-10-electrolytes.stem: Which ECG interval change is associated with low calcium?

choices.text: QT prolongation
choices.explanation: Hypocalcemia tends to prolong QT.

choices.text: Reliable QT shortening
choices.explanation: Shortening is associated with high calcium.

choices.text: Guaranteed loss of every P wave
choices.explanation: This is not the defining calcium effect.

choices.text: A mandatory normal QRS and QT in every patient
choices.explanation: Electrolyte disturbances can change ECG intervals.

ccu-lesson-10-electrolytes.point: Never give potassium as a rapid IV push.
ccu-lesson-10-electrolytes.stem: A potassium prescription is mistakenly prepared for rapid IV push. What should the nurse do?

choices.text: Stop and clarify a safe authorized infusion method
choices.explanation: Rapid IV potassium can cause fatal arrhythmia.

choices.text: Give it rapidly if the patient is monitored
choices.explanation: Monitoring does not make IV push potassium safe.

choices.text: Use a smaller syringe but the same push method
choices.explanation: Syringe size does not remove the hazard.

choices.text: Give it faster if the potassium result is very low
choices.explanation: Severe depletion still requires a controlled replacement plan.

ccu-lesson-11-furosemide.point: Judge decongestion by the patient's respiratory and fluid response.
ccu-lesson-11-furosemide.stem: After furosemide, urine increases but breathlessness worsens. What is the best interpretation?

choices.text: Urine output alone does not establish clinical improvement
choices.explanation: The breathing and full fluid/perfusion picture need reassessment.

choices.text: Any increase in urine proves successful treatment
choices.explanation: The patient can still deteriorate.

choices.text: Worsening dyspnea is the intended effect
choices.explanation: The intended effect is reduced congestion.

choices.text: Further assessment can wait until the bag is empty
choices.explanation: Current deterioration needs attention.

ccu-lesson-11-furosemide.point: Monitor BP, renal function and electrolytes during diuresis.
ccu-lesson-11-furosemide.stem: During diuresis, BP falls, creatinine rises and the patient becomes thirsty. What should be assessed?

choices.text: Possible excessive volume depletion and renal deterioration
choices.explanation: The trend can indicate intolerance of fluid loss.

choices.text: Guaranteed successful decongestion without risk
choices.explanation: These are safety concerns, not proof of uncomplicated benefit.

choices.text: An unrelated skin condition only
choices.explanation: That would not explain the hemodynamic and renal trend.

choices.text: A reason to stop measuring urine output
choices.explanation: Output remains useful in assessing the change.

ccu-lesson-11-furosemide.point: New ectopy during loop diuresis prompts K/Mg review.
ccu-lesson-11-furosemide.stem: A furosemide-treated patient develops frequent PVCs. Which paired tests are most directly relevant?

choices.text: Potassium and magnesium
choices.explanation: Diuretic-related losses can contribute to ectopy.

choices.text: ALT and bilirubin only
choices.explanation: They do not assess the highlighted rhythm mechanism.

choices.text: TSH and free T4 only
choices.explanation: They do not replace immediate electrolyte checks.

choices.text: Platelets and INR only
choices.explanation: They address hemostasis rather than the highlighted electrolyte losses.

ccu-quick-heart-failure.point: Distinguish congestion from poor perfusion in HF.
ccu-quick-heart-failure.stem: An HF patient has both crackles and cold clammy skin. Which interpretation fits?

choices.text: Congestion and poor perfusion may coexist
choices.explanation: The patient can be both wet and cold.

choices.text: Crackles prove organ perfusion is adequate
choices.explanation: Congestion does not guarantee effective output.

choices.text: Cold skin excludes fluid overload
choices.explanation: Both findings can be present together.

choices.text: Only the ankle swelling can determine severity
choices.explanation: The overall respiratory and perfusion picture matters.

ccu-quick-heart-failure.point: Left-sided congestion affects lungs; right-sided congestion affects systemic veins.
ccu-quick-heart-failure.stem: Which pattern most strongly reflects systemic venous congestion?

choices.text: Raised JVP with peripheral edema
choices.explanation: These are characteristic right-sided backup findings.

choices.text: Isolated pulmonary crackles and orthopnea
choices.explanation: These principally reflect pulmonary congestion.

choices.text: New tongue swelling
choices.explanation: This is an airway warning rather than systemic venous congestion.

choices.text: An isolated normal urine test
choices.explanation: It does not define congestion distribution.

ccu-quick-heart-failure.point: Preserved EF does not exclude clinically important HF.
ccu-quick-heart-failure.stem: A patient has preserved EF but substantial orthopnea and congestion. Which statement is appropriate?

choices.text: HF can occur with impaired filling despite preserved EF
choices.explanation: EF alone cannot determine the presence or severity of HF.

choices.text: Preserved EF excludes heart failure
choices.explanation: HFpEF is possible.

choices.text: EF measures the percentage of all body blood in the heart
choices.explanation: It is the fraction of LV blood ejected per contraction.

choices.text: Preserved EF removes the need to assess breathing
choices.explanation: Symptoms and congestion still require assessment.

ccu-quick-heart-failure.point: Escalate acute pulmonary edema or worsening perfusion.
ccu-quick-heart-failure.stem: Which HF change requires urgent escalation?

choices.text: Sudden severe dyspnea with falling BP
choices.explanation: This suggests acute deterioration.

choices.text: Unchanged chronic edema without new symptoms
choices.explanation: It lacks the same acute red flags.

choices.text: An unchanged daily weight with comfortable breathing
choices.explanation: This does not describe acute instability.

choices.text: A request for routine diet advice
choices.explanation: Education can follow urgent clinical priorities.

ccu-quick-dcm.point: Dilated ventricles with weak contraction can lower cardiac output.
ccu-quick-dcm.stem: How does the structural change in DCM contribute to symptoms?

choices.text: Enlarged ventricles contract weakly and reduce effective output
choices.explanation: This links chamber dilation and pump failure.

choices.text: Dilated ventricles always contract more effectively
choices.explanation: Dilation in DCM does not guarantee stronger contraction.

choices.text: DCM affects only the heart's electrical leads
choices.explanation: It is a myocardial structural and functional disorder.

choices.text: A larger chamber guarantees normal organ perfusion
choices.explanation: Size does not establish adequate effective output.

ccu-quick-dcm.point: Monitor DCM for HF, rhythm problems and low-output deterioration.
ccu-quick-dcm.stem: Which new DCM finding needs prompt assessment?

choices.text: Confusion with oliguria and a falling BP
choices.explanation: These suggest low-output organ hypoperfusion.

choices.text: Stable observations with unchanged exercise tolerance
choices.explanation: This does not show new deterioration.

choices.text: An unchanged healed scar
choices.explanation: It is not an acute pump-failure sign.

choices.text: A preference to change appointment time
choices.explanation: This is not a clinical red flag.

ccu-quick-ihd-mi.point: MI is myocardial death from ischemia within the broader IHD spectrum.
ccu-quick-ihd-mi.stem: Which statement correctly relates ischemic heart disease and MI?

choices.text: MI is a specific ischemic event involving myocardial cell death
choices.explanation: IHD is broader than infarction.

choices.text: Every episode of stable angina is an MI
choices.explanation: Ischemia can occur without myocardial necrosis.

choices.text: IHD and MI describe unrelated diseases
choices.explanation: MI belongs to the ischemic spectrum.

choices.text: MI means reduced flow without any cell injury
choices.explanation: Infarction involves myocardial cell death.

ccu-quick-ihd-mi.point: Stable exertional angina does not itself establish infarction.
ccu-quick-ihd-mi.stem: A patient has stable exertional angina. What can be concluded from that diagnosis alone?

choices.text: IHD is present, but MI is not established
choices.explanation: Angina does not by itself prove myocardial necrosis.

choices.text: The patient must be having an acute MI
choices.explanation: Stable angina alone does not establish acute infarction.

choices.text: Coronary blood supply is necessarily normal
choices.explanation: Angina can reflect reduced coronary supply.

choices.text: All future ischemic symptoms can be ignored
choices.explanation: New or changing symptoms still require assessment.

ibd2-lesson-01-fracture-limb-safety.point: Assess distal perfusion, sensation and movement below the injury.
ibd2-lesson-01-fracture-limb-safety.stem: A casted limb becomes more painful. Where should the focused neurovascular check be directed?

choices.text: Distal to the injury, compared with baseline and the other side
choices.explanation: The tissues below the injury may lose perfusion or nerve function.

choices.text: Only the skin above the cast
choices.explanation: This misses the distal neurovascular status.

choices.text: Only the uninjured limb
choices.explanation: Comparison helps, but the injured limb must be assessed.

choices.text: Only the appearance of the cast surface
choices.explanation: An intact cast does not prove tissue safety.

ibd2-lesson-01-fracture-limb-safety.point: A palpable pulse does not exclude compartment syndrome.
ibd2-lesson-01-fracture-limb-safety.stem: Severe increasing pain on passive stretch occurs despite a palpable distal pulse. What is the best interpretation?

choices.text: Compartment syndrome remains an emergency concern
choices.explanation: Pulses may persist while tissue pressure compromises perfusion.

choices.text: A palpable pulse safely excludes compartment syndrome
choices.explanation: Waiting for pulselessness can dangerously delay treatment.

choices.text: Only absent movement justifies escalation
choices.explanation: Motor loss may be a late finding.

choices.text: Passive-stretch pain is always normal after fracture
choices.explanation: Disproportionate worsening pain is an important warning.

ibd2-lesson-01-fracture-limb-safety.point: Recognize and escalate deterioration within supervised intern scope.
ibd2-lesson-01-fracture-limb-safety.stem: An intern suspects compartment syndrome under a cast. What is the appropriate response?

choices.text: Urgently report, reassess and prepare to assist under the authorized plan
choices.explanation: Recognition and escalation are immediate nursing responsibilities.

choices.text: Independently cut all prescribed immobilization without authorization
choices.explanation: Modification requires the applicable order or protocol.

choices.text: Wait for the next routine pain dose before reporting
choices.explanation: Analgesic timing must not delay emergency assessment.

choices.text: Declare the limb safe because the cast is intact
choices.explanation: A structurally intact cast does not exclude tissue compromise.

ibd2-lesson-01-fracture-limb-safety.point: New sensory or motor change strengthens neurovascular concern.
ibd2-lesson-01-fracture-limb-safety.stem: Which new observation most strengthens concern about a worsening injured limb?

choices.text: New tingling with reduced toe movement
choices.explanation: This adds neurological dysfunction to the pain assessment.

choices.text: Unchanged toe sensation and movement
choices.explanation: These do not demonstrate new neurological loss.

choices.text: A clean cast surface
choices.explanation: Surface cleanliness does not assess nerves.

choices.text: A stable appetite
choices.explanation: Appetite does not assess distal neurovascular function.

ibd2-lesson-02-external-fixator.point: Check the limb before the fixation hardware.

choices.text: Pain and distal neurovascular status

choices.text: Pin-site dressings before distal limb assessment
choices.explanation: Wound care matters but must not distract from limb perfusion.

choices.text: Frame alignment without examining the limb
choices.explanation: Hardware appearance does not establish neurovascular safety.

choices.text: The adjustment record before checking new symptoms

ibd2-lesson-02-external-fixator.point: Protect and escalate a loose frame rather than adjusting it independently.
ibd2-lesson-02-external-fixator.stem: A fixator bar appears loose with unexpected movement. What is appropriate?

choices.text: Support the limb, prevent unsafe movement and report

choices.text: Tighten it by feel to match the other bars

choices.text: Ask a visitor to hold the bar while the patient walks

choices.text: Ignore it if the dressing is dry

choices.text: Choose a new cleansing product without checking the plan

choices.text: Accept all new drainage as normal

choices.text: Adjust the pin to release the discharge

ibd2-lesson-02-external-fixator.point: Document and reassess after reporting a limb or frame problem.

choices.text: Only that the frame is present

choices.text: Only the colour of the dressing

choices.text: Nothing until the next shift
